title: BIP-49 P2WPKH-nested addresses
plain: Your seed words — the 12- or 24-word list that controls your bitcoin — get turned into receiving addresses (the long codes you hand out to get paid) by a fixed recipe called a derivation scheme. A wallet, meaning the app or device you use to manage bitcoin, follows that recipe. BIP-49, from May 2016, is one such recipe. A 'BIP' is a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal: a numbered design document. This one is meant for HD wallets — 'hierarchical deterministic' wallets, which grow a whole tree of keys from a single seed. It produces one particular address type: 'P2WPKH nested in P2SH'. Unpacked: Segregated Witness, or 'segwit', is a Bitcoin transaction format defined in BIP-141. 'P2WPKH' stands for 'pay to witness public key hash' — the segwit way of locking coins to one person's public key, the shareable half of a two-part key. 'P2SH' stands for 'pay to script hash' — an older way of locking coins to the fingerprint of a script, which is a mini-program. 'Nested' means the new segwit style is wrapped inside the older style, like a letter inside an envelope, so software from before segwit could still handle the address. BIP-49's big design choice: these addresses live in their own dedicated accounts (labeled sections of a wallet) instead of being mixed into existing ones. Reason: compatibility. Type the same seed words into a wallet that does not understand BIP-49 and that account simply will not appear. That failure is loud and obvious. The rejected alternative — mixing old and new address styles in one account — could make a wallet look fine while quietly missing some of your coins. (Each unspent chunk of bitcoin is called a 'UTXO', or unspent transaction output.) Two takeaways. An empty-looking wallet after you type your seed words in does not prove your coins are gone; the wallet may just not support this account type. And these accounts label their extended public keys — watch-only copies that can see balances but cannot spend — with the prefix 'ypub' instead of the older 'xpub'.
technical: BIP-49 (author Daniel Weigl; assigned 2016-05-19; status Deployed; public domain) defines the derivation scheme for BIP-32 hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallets whose addresses are P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH — BIP-141 segwit pay-to-pubkey-hash outputs wrapped in a BIP-16 pay-to-script-hash. Path: m/purpose'/coin_type'/account'/change/address_index, with purpose = 49' (hardened); all other levels per BIP-44. Construction: witness = <signature> <pubkey>; scriptSig = <0 <20-byte-key-hash>> (0x160014{20-byte-key-hash}); scriptPubKey = HASH160 <20-byte-script-hash> EQUAL (0xA914{20-byte-script-hash}87), the script hash being HASH160 of the serialized scriptSig. Extended keys use alternate version bytes: mainnet 0x049d7cb2 ('ypub', public) and 0x049d7878 ('yprv', private); testnet 0x044a5262 ('upub') and 0x044a4e28 ('uprv'); further prefixes are registered in SLIP-0132. Rationale: for BIP-44-capable wallets the BIP rejects adding segwit addresses to existing accounts (same keys, or branched chains) in favor of dedicated segwit-only accounts, so a BIP-49 masterseed restored into a non-BIP-49 wallet fails visibly — the account is not discovered at all — instead of partially, with UTXOs missed. Backwards compatibility is intentionally absent. Test vectors (testnet, mnemonic 'abandon' eleven times then 'about'): account 0 root m/49'/1'/0'; first receiving key m/49'/1'/0'/0/0, private key cULrpoZGXiuC19Uhvykx7NugygA3k86b3hmdCeyvHYQZSxojGyXJ, keyhash 0x38971f73930f6c141d977ac4fd4a727c854935b3, address 2Mww8dCYPUpKHofjgcXcBCEGmniw9CoaiD2.

claims.claim: BIP-49 defines the derivation scheme for hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallets using the P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH serialization format for segregated witness transactions.
A common derivation scheme lets a user run different HD wallets with the same masterseed, and/or a single account, seamlessly.
The derivation path is m/purpose'/coin_type'/account'/change/address_index with purpose value 49'; all other levels are used as defined in BIP-44.
The scriptSig is <0 <20-byte-key-hash>> (0x160014{20-byte-key-hash}) and the scriptPubKey is HASH160 <20-byte-script-hash> EQUAL (0xA914{20-byte-script-hash}87).
Extended public keys use version bytes 0x049d7cb2 to produce a 'ypub' prefix and extended private keys use 0x049d7878 for 'yprv'; testnet uses 0x044a5262 ('upub') and 0x044a4e28 ('uprv').
Additional registered extended-key version bytes are listed in SLIP-0132.

BIP-49 deliberately uses dedicated segregated-witness-only accounts, so a non-BIP-49-compatible wallet importing the same masterseed either shows the account or not at all, rather than showing it while missing UTXOs.
BIP-49 is not backwards compatible by design; an incompatible wallet will not discover accounts at all.
BIP-49 was authored by Daniel Weigl, assigned 2016-05-19, has status 'Deployed', and is placed in the public domain.
Test vectors use the mnemonic 'abandon' eleven times followed by 'about' on testnet; the first receiving key at m/49'/1'/0'/0/0 derives the testnet address 2Mww8dCYPUpKHofjgcXcBCEGmniw9CoaiD2.

warnings: An empty or missing account after typing in your seed words does not mean the bitcoin is gone — the wallet may not support BIP-49 accounts; do not assume loss and do not discard the seed.
Never use or send funds to the test mnemonic in this spec ('abandon' eleven times, then 'about') — it is public test data and anyone can take money sent to it.
Never share your real seed words with anyone.
source_title: BIP-49: Derivation scheme for P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH based accounts
notes_for_reviewer: Source URL is the canonical bip-0049.mediawiki location in the bitcoin/bips repo; the ingested file was /opt/data/cache/corpus-src/bip-0049.txt — confirm this matches citation policy. All hex bytes, key prefixes, paths, and the testnet address were transcribed exactly; recommend independently re-deriving 2Mww8dCYPUpKHofjgcXcBCEGmniw9CoaiD2, since a single-character error would invalidate the test vector. Context added in plain text beyond the source (flag if strictly-sourced-only wording is required): the xpub-vs-ypub contrast, the rationale that nesting let pre-segwit software handle these addresses, the '12- or 24-word' seed length, and the inference that funds on the public test mnemonic are stealable by anyone. 'Assigned 2016-05-19' is the BIP number assignment date, not segwit activation (2017); plain text says 'from May 2016' on that basis. Staleness risk: nested segwit is a transitional format; most current wallets default to BIP-84 native segwit ('zpub') or BIP-86 taproot — consider companion entries so users can distinguish ypub/zpub/vpub. risk_class set to 'caution' rather than 'danger': the spec contains no destructive procedure, but misreading the compatibility behavior could lead a user to wrongly conclude funds are lost.
